title: HIVE Doctor — Typical Care Pathways (reference)
author: Jeff
safety: Typical care pathways for education only — not a personal prescription or treatment plan. No individual doses are given; for any medicine, follow your label and your prescriber. Your own clinician decides your actual plan, which may differ for good reasons. Emergencies: call your local number (911/112/999). Pending clinician sign-off.
generic_note: No detailed pathway is written for this one yet. Here is the general shape of care — your clinician will tailor it.

uri.confirm: Usually recognised from the story and a quick look at throat, ears and chest; tests are rarely needed.
uri.treatment: Supportive care: rest, fluids, and over-the-counter symptom relief (pain/fever relievers, decongestants, saline rinses). Antibiotics do not help a viral cold.
uri.duration: Most colds ease within 7–10 days; a lingering cough can last 2–3 weeks.
uri.side_effects: OTC decongestants can cause a racing heart or poor sleep; overusing decongestant nose sprays causes rebound congestion.
uri.followup: No routine follow-up needed. Re-check if a high fever returns, breathing gets hard, or symptoms last beyond ~10 days.
uri.recovery: You're better when energy, appetite and breathing are back to normal. See a clinician if it turns into ear, sinus or chest pain.

influenza.confirm: Recognised from sudden fever, aches and cough in flu season; a nasal swab can confirm it if it changes treatment.
influenza.treatment: Rest, fluids and fever/pain relief. Antiviral medicine (a neuraminidase-type, e.g. oseltamivir-class) may be offered early, especially if you're high-risk.
influenza.duration: The worst usually passes in 3–5 days; full energy can take 1–2 weeks.
influenza.side_effects: Antivirals can cause nausea; fever relievers can upset the stomach if taken without food.
influenza.followup: Re-check if you improve then worsen again (possible chest infection), or if breathing becomes difficult.
influenza.recovery: Recovered when fever is gone for 24h without medicine and you can do normal activity. High-risk people should have a low threshold to be seen.

covid.confirm: A rapid antigen or PCR test confirms it; a clinician checks oxygen levels if breathing is a concern.
covid.treatment: Rest, fluids, fever/pain relief. Antiviral pills may be offered early to higher-risk people. Oxygen or hospital care only if levels drop.
covid.duration: Most mild cases improve over 5–10 days; some symptoms (taste, fatigue) can linger.
covid.side_effects: Antivirals can interact with other medicines and may cause an odd taste or stomach upset — pharmacist should check your list.
covid.followup: Watch oxygen if you have a monitor; re-check for worsening breathlessness or chest pain.
covid.recovery: Better when fever settles and energy returns. Persistent or new breathlessness, or symptoms dragging past a few weeks, deserves a review.

bronchitis.confirm: Diagnosed from a cough after a cold with a clear chest exam; a chest X-ray is used only to rule out pneumonia.
bronchitis.treatment: Mostly supportive — fluids, rest, honey or cough soothers. Antibiotics usually don't help unless a bacterial infection is found.
bronchitis.duration: The cough commonly lasts 2–3 weeks even once you feel otherwise well.
bronchitis.side_effects: Cough medicines can cause drowsiness; antibiotics (if given) can cause stomach upset or thrush.
bronchitis.followup: Re-check if you develop fever and breathlessness, cough up blood, or the cough lasts beyond 3–4 weeks.
bronchitis.recovery: Resolved when the cough fades and breathing is easy. A cough past 8 weeks needs further assessment.

sinusitis.confirm: Based on facial pain/pressure, blocked nose and discharge; imaging is reserved for severe or recurring cases.
sinusitis.treatment: Saline rinses, steam, decongestants and pain relief. A steroid nasal spray helps many. Antibiotics only if it's severe or not settling after ~10 days.
sinusitis.duration: Viral sinusitis usually clears in 1–2 weeks.
sinusitis.side_effects: Decongestant sprays cause rebound stuffiness if used more than a few days; steroid sprays can cause minor nosebleeds.
sinusitis.followup: Re-check for swelling around the eye, severe headache, or symptoms lasting beyond 10 days (may need antibiotics).
sinusitis.recovery: Better when pressure and discharge clear. Frequent return warrants an ENT review.

strep.confirm: A throat swab or rapid strep test confirms it — important because it looks like a viral sore throat.
strep.treatment: A full course of penicillin-class antibiotic (or an alternative if allergic) plus pain/fever relief. Finish the whole course.
strep.duration: Fever and pain usually improve within 1–2 days of antibiotics; the course runs about 10 days.
strep.side_effects: Antibiotics can cause diarrhoea, rash or thrush; tell your prescriber about any penicillin allergy.
strep.followup: Re-check if not improving in 2–3 days, or if rash, joint pain or dark urine appear.
strep.recovery: No longer contagious after ~24h of antibiotics and when you feel well. Completing the course protects the heart and kidneys.

tonsillitis.confirm: Exam of the throat; a swab sorts bacterial (strep) from viral causes.
tonsillitis.treatment: Pain/fever relief and fluids for viral cases; antibiotics when strep is confirmed. Surgery (tonsillectomy) only for frequent, disabling attacks.
tonsillitis.duration: Symptoms usually settle within a week.
tonsillitis.side_effects: Same as antibiotics above; strong painkillers can cause constipation.
tonsillitis.followup: Re-check for drooling, trouble opening the mouth, or one-sided swelling (possible abscess — urgent).
tonsillitis.recovery: Recovered when swallowing is comfortable. Repeated attacks each year is the trigger for an ENT discussion.

pneumonia.confirm: Confirmed with a chest exam, oxygen reading and usually a chest X-ray; bloods may be taken.
pneumonia.treatment: Antibiotics (class chosen by the clinician), fluids, rest and fever relief. More severe cases need hospital care and oxygen.
pneumonia.duration: Mild pneumonia improves over 1–2 weeks; tiredness and cough can linger 4–6 weeks.
pneumonia.side_effects: Antibiotics can cause stomach upset or diarrhoea; report any rash or breathing trouble.
pneumonia.followup: A review and sometimes a repeat X-ray at 6 weeks to confirm clearing, especially in smokers and older adults.
pneumonia.recovery: Better as fever, breathlessness and appetite normalise. Seek urgent care for rising breathlessness, confusion or blue lips.

asthma_exac.confirm: Recognised from wheeze, cough and tight chest; a peak-flow or oxygen reading grades severity.
asthma_exac.treatment: Reliever inhaler (short-acting bronchodilator) through a spacer, often a short steroid course, and an urgent review. Severe attacks need emergency care.
asthma_exac.duration: A mild flare settles over days with treatment; the steroid course is usually short.
asthma_exac.side_effects: Reliever inhalers can cause shakiness and a fast heart; steroid tablets can disturb sleep and mood over a short course.
asthma_exac.followup: Review within 48h of a flare, and an asthma-plan check to adjust the preventer inhaler.
asthma_exac.recovery: Controlled when you need the reliever rarely and sleep isn't broken by symptoms. Call emergency services if the reliever isn't working or speaking is hard.

copd_exac.confirm: From worsening breathlessness, sputum change and oxygen level in someone with known COPD.
copd_exac.treatment: Increased inhalers/nebuliser, often a short steroid course, antibiotics if sputum is infected, and oxygen if levels are low.
copd_exac.duration: A flare typically improves over 1–2 weeks with treatment.
copd_exac.side_effects: Steroids can raise blood sugar and disturb sleep short-term; inhalers can cause tremor and dry mouth.
copd_exac.followup: Review to confirm recovery and optimise the inhaler/rescue-pack plan; pulmonary rehab helps.
copd_exac.recovery: Back to your usual baseline breathing. Seek urgent help for severe breathlessness, drowsiness or blue lips.

allergic_rhinitis.confirm: Clinical — sneezing, itch and a clear runny nose with seasonal or trigger pattern; allergy testing only if unclear.
allergic_rhinitis.treatment: Avoid triggers, non-drowsy antihistamines, and a steroid nasal spray (the most effective single treatment). Saline rinses help.
allergic_rhinitis.duration: Relief within days; nasal sprays work best after a week of regular use and through the season.
allergic_rhinitis.side_effects: Older antihistamines cause drowsiness; steroid sprays can cause minor nosebleeds or throat irritation.
allergic_rhinitis.followup: Review if symptoms aren't controlled — technique and add-on treatments can be adjusted.
allergic_rhinitis.recovery: Well-controlled means clear nose and eyes on treatment. Persistent one-sided symptoms should be checked.

croup.confirm: Recognised from a barking cough and harsh noisy breathing in a young child; usually a clinical diagnosis.
croup.treatment: Calm the child; a single dose of steroid (clinician-given) settles most. Severe cases need hospital nebulised adrenaline and oxygen.
croup.duration: The barking cough usually eases within a few days.
croup.side_effects: The steroid dose is single and well-tolerated; report any worsening stridor.
croup.followup: Re-check urgently for noisy breathing at rest, drooling, or the child struggling to breathe.
croup.recovery: Better when breathing is quiet and the child is feeding and playing. Night symptoms often ease with cool air.

gerd.confirm: Often diagnosed from typical burning reflux; a trial of acid suppression confirms it. Endoscopy if alarm features (weight loss, swallowing trouble, bleeding).
gerd.treatment: Smaller meals, avoiding late eating and triggers, raising the bed head, weight loss if relevant, plus antacids or an acid-reducing medicine (H2 blocker or proton-pump inhibitor).
gerd.duration: Symptoms often improve within 1–2 weeks; acid-reducers are reviewed after about 4–8 weeks.
gerd.side_effects: PPIs can cause headache or bowel changes and aren't meant for indefinite use without review; antacids can affect other medicines' absorption.
gerd.followup: Review at 4–8 weeks to step down treatment; endoscopy if symptoms persist or alarm features appear.
gerd.recovery: Controlled when reflux is occasional on lifestyle measures. New swallowing trouble or weight loss needs prompt review.

gastritis_ulcer.confirm: Suspected from gnawing upper-tummy pain; tested for H. pylori (breath/stool) and sometimes endoscopy.
gastritis_ulcer.treatment: Acid-reducing medicine (PPI), stopping anti-inflammatory painkillers and smoking, and a specific antibiotic course if H. pylori is found.
gastritis_ulcer.duration: Pain often eases within 1–2 weeks; ulcers heal over 4–8 weeks on treatment.
gastritis_ulcer.side_effects: PPIs as above; the H. pylori antibiotic course can cause a metallic taste, nausea and must avoid alcohol.
gastritis_ulcer.followup: Confirm H. pylori clearance after treatment; repeat endoscopy for stomach ulcers to confirm healing.
gastritis_ulcer.recovery: Healed when pain is gone and any infection cleared. Black stools, vomiting blood or sudden severe pain are emergencies.

gastroenteritis.confirm: Clinical — vomiting and/or diarrhoea, usually viral; stool tests only for severe, bloody or prolonged cases.
gastroenteritis.treatment: The priority is fluids and salts (oral rehydration). Eat as tolerated. Anti-sickness or anti-diarrhoea medicine occasionally; antibiotics only for specific infections.
gastroenteritis.duration: Most cases settle in 2–4 days; diarrhoea can lag a few extra days.
gastroenteritis.side_effects: Anti-diarrhoea medicines aren't used if there's high fever or blood in stool; rehydration salts are the safest mainstay.
gastroenteritis.followup: Re-check for signs of dehydration (little urine, dizziness), blood in stool, or symptoms beyond a week.
gastroenteritis.recovery: Recovered when you keep fluids down and bowels normalise. Babies, older and frail people dehydrate fast — lower threshold to be seen.

ibs.confirm: A positive clinical diagnosis from the pattern, after simple tests rule out coeliac, infection and inflammation.
ibs.treatment: Diet adjustments (fibre tuning, a trial low-FODMAP approach with guidance), stress management, and medicines aimed at the main symptom (cramp, constipation or diarrhoea).
ibs.duration: A long-term condition managed in flares; diet changes show effect over several weeks.
ibs.side_effects: Antispasmodics can cause dry mouth; laxatives or anti-diarrhoeals are matched to the symptom and adjusted.
ibs.followup: Review after a diet trial to see what helped; re-check if weight loss, bleeding or night symptoms appear (not typical of IBS).
ibs.recovery: Managed when flares are fewer and milder. New alarm symptoms always warrant re-assessment.

constipation.confirm: Clinical; tests only if there are alarm features (bleeding, weight loss, new onset in older adults).
constipation.treatment: More fluid, fibre and movement first; then a laxative (bulk, osmotic or stimulant) chosen for the situation. Review medicines that constipate.
constipation.duration: Improvement over days to a couple of weeks as habits and laxatives take effect.
constipation.side_effects: Stimulant laxatives can cause cramps; osmotic ones can cause bloating — the type is adjusted to comfort.
constipation.followup: Re-check for a persistent change in bowel habit, bleeding, or weight loss.
constipation.recovery: Resolved when stools are soft and regular without straining. Persistent change over weeks needs assessment.

hemorrhoids.confirm: Diagnosed on examination; a clinician checks there's no other cause of bleeding.
hemorrhoids.treatment: Fibre, fluids and not straining; soothing creams and short courses of topical treatment. Procedures (banding) or surgery for stubborn cases.
hemorrhoids.duration: Flares often settle within 1–2 weeks with self-care.
hemorrhoids.side_effects: Steroid-containing creams are used only short-term to avoid skin thinning.
hemorrhoids.followup: Re-check if bleeding continues, there's a change in bowel habit, or you're over 40 with new bleeding (needs assessment).
hemorrhoids.recovery: Better as bleeding and lumps settle. Don't assume all rectal bleeding is piles — new or persistent bleeding is checked properly.

gallstones.confirm: Confirmed with an ultrasound; bloods check the liver and for infection.
gallstones.treatment: Pain relief and avoiding fatty triggers for simple colic; keyhole gallbladder removal is the definitive treatment for recurrent or complicated stones.
gallstones.duration: An attack settles over hours; surgery is planned electively unless there's infection.
gallstones.side_effects: Strong painkillers can cause nausea and constipation; after surgery some people have looser stools for a while.
gallstones.followup: Surgical review to plan removal; urgent return for fever, jaundice or constant severe pain (infection/blockage).
gallstones.recovery: Resolved once the gallbladder is removed or attacks stop. Fever with the pain means possible infection — be seen urgently.

appendicitis.confirm: Suspected from migrating right-lower-tummy pain; confirmed with exam, bloods and ultrasound or CT.
appendicitis.treatment: This usually needs surgery (appendix removal) with antibiotics; some selected cases are treated with antibiotics alone in hospital.
appendicitis.duration: Recovery after keyhole surgery is typically 1–2 weeks.
appendicitis.side_effects: Post-op: wound soreness, temporary bowel sluggishness; antibiotics can upset the stomach.
appendicitis.followup: Wound check and return if fever, spreading pain or wound redness develop.
appendicitis.recovery: Recovered when eating, moving and wounds heal. Sudden severe worsening before surgery can mean rupture — emergency care.

diverticulitis.confirm: Suspected from left-lower-tummy pain and fever; confirmed with bloods and CT.
diverticulitis.treatment: Mild cases: rest, fluids and sometimes antibiotics as an outpatient. Severe cases need hospital antibiotics; abscesses or perforation need drainage or surgery.
diverticulitis.duration: Mild flares improve over about a week.
diverticulitis.side_effects: Antibiotics can cause diarrhoea; a temporary lower-fibre diet is used during the acute flare then fibre is increased.
diverticulitis.followup: A colonoscopy is usually arranged weeks later to check the bowel once settled.
diverticulitis.recovery: Resolved when pain and fever clear. Increasing pain, high fever or inability to pass stool/gas needs urgent review.

hepatitis.confirm: From jaundice, fatigue and liver blood tests; viral screens, ultrasound and medication/alcohol review find the cause.
hepatitis.treatment: Depends on cause: rest and supportive care for many viral cases, specific antivirals for hepatitis B/C, and removing the trigger (alcohol, a medicine).
hepatitis.duration: Acute viral hepatitis often improves over weeks; chronic forms need long-term specialist care.
hepatitis.side_effects: Antivirals are specialist-monitored; avoid alcohol and check every medicine (even paracetamol dose) with your clinician.
hepatitis.followup: Repeat liver tests to confirm recovery and specialist referral for chronic infection.
hepatitis.recovery: Recovered when liver tests normalise and energy returns. Confusion, severe vomiting or deepening jaundice needs urgent care.

celiac.confirm: Blood antibody tests while still eating gluten, confirmed by a gut biopsy.
celiac.treatment: A strict lifelong gluten-free diet is the whole treatment; a dietitian helps, and deficiencies (iron, B12, vitamin D) are corrected.
celiac.duration: Symptoms improve over weeks to months once gluten is removed; the gut lining heals over months.
celiac.side_effects: No drug side effects — the challenge is label-reading and avoiding hidden gluten and cross-contamination.
celiac.followup: Repeat antibodies and nutrient checks to confirm healing and adherence; bone-density check over time.
celiac.recovery: Well when symptoms resolve and antibodies normalise on a gluten-free diet. Accidental gluten causes a temporary relapse.

uti.confirm: A urine dipstick and sometimes a culture confirm infection and guide the antibiotic.
uti.treatment: A short antibiotic course for confirmed infection, plus fluids and pain relief. Simple cases in women are often treated on symptoms.
uti.duration: Symptoms usually improve within 1–2 days; the course is typically short (3 days for simple cases).
uti.side_effects: Antibiotics can cause thrush, nausea or rash; drink plenty of fluids.
uti.followup: Re-check if no better in 48h, if there's back pain and fever (kidney infection), or infections keep returning.
uti.recovery: Resolved when burning and urgency clear. Men, children and pregnancy need a culture and closer follow-up.

pyelonephritis.confirm: From flank pain, fever and urine findings; bloods, culture and sometimes imaging.
pyelonephritis.treatment: A longer antibiotic course; fluids and pain/fever relief. Severe cases or vomiting need hospital IV antibiotics.
pyelonephritis.duration: Fever settles over 2–3 days on the right antibiotic; the course runs 7–14 days.
pyelonephritis.side_effects: Antibiotics as above; report worsening pain or persistent fever.
pyelonephritis.followup: Follow-up to confirm clearance and, for recurring cases, imaging to check for stones or obstruction.
pyelonephritis.recovery: Better as fever and flank pain clear. Not improving in 48–72h, or feeling very unwell, means urgent reassessment.

kidney_stone.confirm: Confirmed with a CT (or ultrasound); urine checked for blood and infection.
kidney_stone.treatment: Strong pain relief (anti-inflammatory type often first), fluids, and a medicine to help small stones pass. Larger stones may need shockwave treatment or a scope procedure.
kidney_stone.duration: Many small stones pass within 1–4 weeks.
kidney_stone.side_effects: Anti-inflammatory painkillers can irritate the stomach and aren't for everyone; the stone-passing medicine can cause dizziness.
kidney_stone.followup: Review to check the stone passed and, for recurrent stones, tests to prevent new ones.
kidney_stone.recovery: Resolved when the stone passes and pain stops. Fever with a stone is an emergency (blocked, infected kidney).

bph.confirm: From urinary symptoms in older men; exam, urine test, a PSA discussion and flow assessment.
bph.treatment: Watchful waiting for mild cases; medicines that relax the prostate (alpha-blockers) or shrink it (5-alpha-reductase type). Surgery for severe or complicated cases.
bph.duration: Alpha-blockers help within days; shrinking medicines take months.
bph.side_effects: Alpha-blockers can cause dizziness on standing and affect ejaculation; shrinking medicines can lower libido.
bph.followup: Review symptom scores and rule out other causes; sudden inability to pass urine is an emergency.
bph.recovery: Managed when flow and night-time trips improve. Blood in urine or complete retention needs prompt assessment.

prostatitis.confirm: From pelvic/perineal pain and urinary symptoms; urine tests and exam; bloods if feverish.
prostatitis.treatment: A longer antibiotic course for bacterial cases, pain relief, and measures for chronic pelvic pain. Acute severe cases may need hospital care.
prostatitis.duration: Acute cases improve over days but the antibiotic course is often 2–4 weeks.
prostatitis.side_effects: Long antibiotic courses can cause gut upset and thrush; chronic cases may need combined approaches.
prostatitis.followup: Review to confirm clearance; chronic pelvic pain benefits from a broader plan.
prostatitis.recovery: Better as pain and urinary symptoms settle. High fever and feeling very unwell means urgent care.

sti_urethritis.confirm: Confirmed with urine or swab tests; partners are tested too.
sti_urethritis.treatment: Targeted antibiotics for the specific infection, given by a sexual-health service; avoiding sex until treated and partners managed.
sti_urethritis.duration: Symptoms usually clear within about a week of the right treatment.
sti_urethritis.side_effects: Antibiotics can cause stomach upset; a test-of-cure is done for certain infections.
sti_urethritis.followup: Partner notification and re-testing as advised; a full sexual-health screen is offered.
sti_urethritis.recovery: Resolved when symptoms clear and tests confirm cure. Confidential care is the norm — being seen early prevents complications.

pid.confirm: From pelvic pain and tenderness in women; swabs, pregnancy test and sometimes ultrasound.
pid.treatment: A combination antibiotic course started promptly (often before results) to protect fertility; pain relief; partner treatment.
pid.duration: Symptoms improve over days; the antibiotic course runs about 2 weeks.
pid.side_effects: Combination antibiotics can cause nausea and thrush; avoid alcohol with certain ones.
pid.followup: Review at 48–72h to confirm improvement; re-check if not better (may need hospital care).
pid.recovery: Better as pain and fever settle. Early treatment matters because delay risks fertility; severe pain or fever needs urgent care.

migraine.confirm: A clinical diagnosis from the pattern; scans only if there are red-flag features.
migraine.treatment: Treat attacks early with pain relievers or a triptan, rest in a dark room, and anti-sickness medicine. Frequent attacks: preventers and trigger/lifestyle work.
migraine.duration: An attack lasts 4–72 hours; preventers take 6–8 weeks to show benefit.
migraine.side_effects: Triptans can cause chest tightness or tingling and aren't for everyone; overusing acute painkillers causes medication-overuse headache.
migraine.followup: Keep a headache diary; review preventers after a couple of months. Re-check for any new neurological change.
migraine.recovery: Controlled when attacks are fewer and respond to treatment. A sudden 'worst-ever' headache is an emergency.

tension_ha.confirm: Clinical — a band-like, pressing headache without migraine features.
tension_ha.treatment: Simple pain relief used sparingly, posture and screen breaks, hydration, sleep and stress management.
tension_ha.duration: Individual headaches settle in hours; the pattern improves as triggers are addressed.
tension_ha.side_effects: Frequent painkiller use (more than ~2 days/week) can itself cause rebound headaches.
tension_ha.followup: Review if headaches become frequent or change in character.
tension_ha.recovery: Better as frequency drops with lifestyle measures. New features (fever, weakness, visual loss) change the picture and need review.

vertigo.confirm: From the spinning pattern and bedside tests; the clinician checks it's inner-ear, not central.
vertigo.treatment: For BPPV, specific repositioning manoeuvres (e.g. Epley) are highly effective; short courses of anti-sickness medicine for bad spells; balance exercises.
vertigo.duration: BPPV often resolves within days to a few weeks, sometimes in one session of manoeuvres.
vertigo.side_effects: Anti-sickness/vertigo medicines cause drowsiness and are used only short-term (they slow recovery if overused).
vertigo.followup: Review if it persists, recurs, or comes with hearing loss, weakness or slurred speech (needs urgent assessment).
vertigo.recovery: Recovered when the spinning stops and balance returns. Sudden vertigo with neurological signs is treated as an emergency.

sciatica.confirm: From leg pain in a nerve pattern; exam. Imaging (MRI) only if severe, persistent, or red flags.
sciatica.treatment: Stay active, pain relief (anti-inflammatory and/or nerve-pain medicine), and physiotherapy. Injections or surgery for stubborn or severe nerve compression.
sciatica.duration: Most cases improve substantially over 4–6 weeks.
sciatica.side_effects: Nerve-pain medicines can cause drowsiness and dizziness and are increased slowly; anti-inflammatories can irritate the stomach.
sciatica.followup: Review at a few weeks; urgent review for leg weakness, numbness in the saddle area, or bladder/bowel changes.
sciatica.recovery: Better as pain eases and movement returns. Saddle numbness or loss of bladder control is an emergency (cauda equina).

concussion.confirm: A clinical diagnosis after a head injury; a CT scan is used if there are warning features.
concussion.treatment: Physical and mental rest at first, then a gradual, stepwise return to activity and screens; simple pain relief for headache.
concussion.duration: Most people recover within 2 weeks; some symptoms linger longer.
concussion.side_effects: Avoid alcohol and sedatives early; reintroduce exercise gradually to avoid setbacks.
concussion.followup: Re-check for worsening headache, repeated vomiting, drowsiness, confusion or weakness (urgent).
concussion.recovery: Recovered when symptoms clear at rest and with activity. No return to contact sport until fully symptom-free and cleared.

bells_palsy.confirm: A clinical diagnosis of one-sided facial weakness after ruling out stroke and other causes.
bells_palsy.treatment: A steroid course started early improves recovery; eye protection (drops, taping at night) is essential while the eye won't close.
bells_palsy.duration: Most people start recovering within 2–3 weeks and many fully recover over 3–6 months.
bells_palsy.side_effects: Short steroid courses can disturb sleep and mood and raise blood sugar temporarily.
bells_palsy.followup: Review to confirm recovery; refer if no improvement or if the eye is at risk.
bells_palsy.recovery: Recovered as facial movement returns. Protecting the eye prevents lasting damage; sudden onset is checked urgently to exclude stroke.

stroke.confirm: An emergency — recognised with the FAST signs and confirmed by an urgent brain scan in hospital.
stroke.treatment: Time-critical hospital treatment: clot-busting medicine or clot-removal for suitable clots, then a stroke-unit, rehabilitation and prevention medicines.
stroke.duration: Treatment windows are measured in hours; rehabilitation continues for weeks to months.
stroke.side_effects: Clot-busting carries a bleeding risk weighed by the stroke team; prevention medicines (blood thinners, blood-pressure and cholesterol drugs) have their own monitoring.
stroke.followup: Structured rehab and a prevention plan (blood pressure, rhythm, cholesterol, lifestyle) with regular review.
stroke.recovery: The priority is calling emergency services at the first sign — 'time is brain'. Do not wait to see if it passes.

low_back.confirm: Usually a clinical diagnosis; imaging only for red flags or pain that won't settle.
low_back.treatment: Stay active and keep moving, short-term pain relief, heat, and exercises/physiotherapy. Bed rest is discouraged.
low_back.duration: Most episodes improve markedly within 2–6 weeks.
low_back.side_effects: Anti-inflammatory painkillers can irritate the stomach; muscle relaxants cause drowsiness and are short-term.
low_back.followup: Review if no better after 6 weeks; urgent review for leg weakness, saddle numbness or bladder/bowel changes.
low_back.recovery: Better as movement and comfort return. Building core strength and activity reduces future episodes.

sprain.confirm: Clinical; an X-ray only if a fracture is suspected (unable to weight-bear, bony tenderness).
sprain.treatment: The PRICE approach — protect, rest, ice, compression, elevation — early, then gentle movement and strengthening. Pain relief as needed.
sprain.duration: Mild sprains settle in 1–2 weeks; more severe ones take 4–6 weeks.
sprain.side_effects: Ice is used for short periods to avoid skin damage; avoid heavy loading too early.
sprain.followup: Review if you can't bear weight, it's not improving, or the joint feels unstable.
sprain.recovery: Recovered when the joint is pain-free, strong and stable. Returning to sport too soon risks re-injury.

fracture.confirm: Confirmed with an X-ray (sometimes CT); the clinician checks blood flow and nerves around it.
fracture.treatment: Realignment if needed, then a cast, splint or surgery (pins/plates) depending on the break; pain relief throughout.
fracture.duration: Most simple fractures heal over 6–8 weeks; some take longer.
fracture.side_effects: Immobilisation can stiffen the joint — physiotherapy follows; watch a cast for tightness, numbness or colour change.
fracture.followup: Repeat X-rays to confirm healing and a rehab plan to restore strength and movement.
fracture.recovery: Healed when the bone is solid on X-ray and function returns. Increasing pain, numbness or a cold limb in a cast is urgent.

gout.confirm: From the sudden hot, swollen joint; confirmed by joint-fluid crystals or a raised urate blood level.
gout.treatment: For an attack: anti-inflammatory medicine, colchicine, or a short steroid course, plus rest. Long-term: urate-lowering medicine for recurrent attacks.
gout.duration: An attack settles over about a week with treatment; urate-lowering therapy is long-term.
gout.side_effects: Colchicine commonly causes diarrhoea; anti-inflammatories can affect the stomach and kidneys; urate-lowering drugs can trigger a flare when first started.
gout.followup: Review to decide on prevention; blood tests to reach a urate target and protect joints and kidneys.
gout.recovery: Controlled when attacks stop and urate is in target range. Diet and alcohol moderation help, but medicine does the heavy lifting.

osteoarthritis.confirm: From the pattern and exam; X-rays support it but severity on scans doesn't always match symptoms.
osteoarthritis.treatment: Exercise and weight management (the most effective measures), pain relief (topical first, then oral), and joint replacement for severe, limiting cases.
osteoarthritis.duration: A long-term condition managed over years; exercise benefits build over weeks.
osteoarthritis.side_effects: Oral anti-inflammatories carry stomach, kidney and heart cautions with long use — topical forms are preferred where possible.
osteoarthritis.followup: Review to adjust pain control and refer for surgery when daily life is badly limited.
osteoarthritis.recovery: Managed when pain allows normal activity. Staying strong and active protects the joints better than rest.

ra.confirm: From the pattern of joint swelling; bloods (inflammation markers, antibodies) and sometimes imaging; a rheumatologist confirms.
ra.treatment: Disease-modifying medicines (DMARDs such as methotrexate-class) started early to protect joints, with steroids to bridge flares; physiotherapy.
ra.duration: DMARDs take 6–12 weeks to work fully; this is long-term specialist care.
ra.side_effects: DMARDs need regular blood monitoring (liver, blood counts) and raise infection risk; steroids have their own effects.
ra.followup: Regular rheumatology review and blood tests to track disease activity and medicine safety.
ra.recovery: Controlled when joints are not swollen and function is preserved. Early treatment prevents joint damage.

plantar_fasciitis.confirm: A clinical diagnosis from first-step heel pain; imaging rarely needed.
plantar_fasciitis.treatment: Calf and foot stretches, supportive footwear and insoles, activity modification, and pain relief; injections or other treatments for stubborn cases.
plantar_fasciitis.duration: Often improves over weeks to a few months with consistent stretching.
plantar_fasciitis.side_effects: Steroid injections are limited in number (can weaken the fascia); anti-inflammatories carry the usual cautions.
plantar_fasciitis.followup: Review if no better after a few months of self-care.
plantar_fasciitis.recovery: Better as morning pain fades with stretching and good footwear. Patience and consistency are the main treatment.

carpal_tunnel.confirm: From hand tingling in a nerve pattern; confirmed with nerve-conduction tests if surgery is considered.
carpal_tunnel.treatment: A night wrist splint first, activity changes, sometimes a steroid injection; a small release operation for persistent or severe cases.
carpal_tunnel.duration: Splinting helps over weeks; surgery gives lasting relief when needed.
carpal_tunnel.side_effects: Injections can cause temporary pain; after surgery there's short-term soreness and a few weeks' recovery.
carpal_tunnel.followup: Review if numbness is constant or the hand is weakening (don't delay surgery if the nerve is at risk).
carpal_tunnel.recovery: Better as tingling and night symptoms settle. Constant numbness or muscle wasting means the nerve needs prompt attention.

cellulitis.confirm: A clinical diagnosis of a spreading, hot, red area; the border is often marked to track it; bloods if feverish.
cellulitis.treatment: Antibiotics (oral for mild, IV in hospital for severe), elevation of the limb, and pain relief. The source (e.g. athlete's foot, a cut) is treated too.
cellulitis.duration: Redness should start settling within 2–3 days of antibiotics; the course runs about a week.
cellulitis.side_effects: Antibiotics can cause gut upset or thrush; redness can briefly look worse before it improves.
cellulitis.followup: Review at 48h to confirm it's improving; urgent return if it spreads past the marked line, or with fever and feeling very unwell.
cellulitis.recovery: Resolved when redness, heat and swelling clear. Rapidly spreading redness, severe pain or feeling very unwell needs urgent care.

shingles.confirm: A clinical diagnosis from the one-sided blistering rash in a band; swabs only if unclear.
shingles.treatment: Antiviral medicine started early (ideally within 72h), pain relief (including nerve-pain medicine if needed), and keeping the rash clean.
shingles.duration: The rash crusts over 7–10 days; nerve pain can linger weeks to months in some.
shingles.side_effects: Antivirals need plenty of fluids; nerve-pain medicines cause drowsiness and are increased slowly.
shingles.followup: Review for severe pain, rash near the eye (urgent), or widespread rash.
shingles.recovery: Better as blisters crust and pain fades. A rash near the eye or in someone immune-suppressed needs urgent attention.

urticaria.confirm: A clinical diagnosis of raised itchy weals; tests only for persistent or triggered cases.
urticaria.treatment: Non-drowsy antihistamines (sometimes at higher clinician-directed doses), avoiding triggers, and a short steroid course for severe flares.
urticaria.duration: Acute hives often settle within days to weeks; chronic forms are managed longer.
urticaria.side_effects: Older antihistamines cause drowsiness; the newer ones are preferred by day.
urticaria.followup: Review if hives persist beyond 6 weeks or come with swelling of lips/tongue or breathing trouble (emergency).
urticaria.recovery: Resolved when weals stop appearing. Throat/tongue swelling or breathing difficulty is anaphylaxis — call emergency services.

eczema.confirm: A clinical diagnosis from the itchy, dry, flaring rash in typical sites.
eczema.treatment: Frequent emollients (the foundation), topical steroids for flares matched to body area, trigger avoidance, and treating any skin infection.
eczema.duration: Flares settle over days to weeks with treatment; it's a long-term relapsing condition.
eczema.side_effects: Topical steroids used correctly are safe; overuse on the face/folds can thin skin, so strength is matched to the site.
eczema.followup: Review if not controlled, if the skin becomes weepy/crusted (infection), or for a stepped-up plan.
eczema.recovery: Controlled when skin is comfortable and flares are infrequent. Daily moisturising even when clear prevents flares.

abscess.confirm: A clinical diagnosis of a tender, fluctuant lump; ultrasound if deep.
abscess.treatment: The main treatment is drainage (incision) of the pus; antibiotics if surrounding infection or fever. Pain relief and dressing changes after.
abscess.duration: Pain eases quickly after drainage; the cavity heals over 1–2 weeks with dressings.
abscess.side_effects: Antibiotics (if used) can upset the stomach; the wound is left to heal from the base with packing/dressings.
abscess.followup: Wound review and dressing changes; return for spreading redness or fever.
abscess.recovery: Healed when the cavity closes and redness clears. Drainage, not antibiotics alone, is usually what cures an abscess.

impetigo.confirm: A clinical diagnosis from the golden-crusted sores; a swab if widespread or not clearing.
impetigo.treatment: Topical antibiotic or antiseptic for localised cases; oral antibiotics if widespread. Good hygiene to limit spread.
impetigo.duration: Usually clears within about a week of treatment.
impetigo.side_effects: Topical antibiotics can irritate; oral ones can upset the stomach.
impetigo.followup: Keep off school/work until crusts heal or 48h of antibiotics; review if spreading or not improving.
impetigo.recovery: Resolved when sores crust and heal. It's contagious — separate towels and good handwashing matter.

acne.confirm: A clinical diagnosis graded by severity and type (blackheads, spots, cysts).
acne.treatment: Topical treatments (benzoyl peroxide, retinoids, antibiotic combos) for mild/moderate; oral antibiotics or hormonal treatment for moderate; specialist oral retinoid for severe.
acne.duration: Treatments take 6–8 weeks to show benefit and months for full effect.
acne.side_effects: Topicals cause dryness and sun sensitivity; oral retinoids need specialist monitoring and strict pregnancy precautions.
acne.followup: Review at 2–3 months to judge response and step treatment up or down.
acne.recovery: Improved when spots and inflammation settle; consistency is key, and scarring is prevented by treating early.

ringworm.confirm: A clinical diagnosis from the ring-shaped scaly patch; a skin scraping if unclear.
ringworm.treatment: Topical antifungal cream for skin; antifungal tablets for scalp or nail involvement. Keep the area clean and dry.
ringworm.duration: Skin ringworm usually clears in 2–4 weeks; nails and scalp take months.
ringworm.side_effects: Topical antifungals can irritate; oral antifungals need liver monitoring for long courses.
ringworm.followup: Review if not improving or if scalp/nails are involved (need tablets).
ringworm.recovery: Resolved when the rash clears; continue cream a little past clearing to prevent return. It's contagious by contact.

contact_dermatitis.confirm: A clinical diagnosis from the pattern; patch testing identifies the allergen in persistent cases.
contact_dermatitis.treatment: Identify and avoid the trigger, emollients, and a topical steroid for the flare; barrier protection (e.g. gloves) where relevant.
contact_dermatitis.duration: Settles over 1–3 weeks once the trigger is removed.
contact_dermatitis.side_effects: Topical steroid cautions as above — matched to the body area and used short-term for flares.
contact_dermatitis.followup: Review if it keeps returning (patch testing) or becomes infected.
contact_dermatitis.recovery: Resolved when the rash clears and the trigger is avoided. Finding the cause is what prevents recurrence.

new_diabetes.confirm: Confirmed with blood glucose and HbA1c tests; type is determined with further tests.
new_diabetes.treatment: Type 2: lifestyle (diet, activity, weight) plus medicines (often metformin-class first). Type 1: insulin from diagnosis. Education and glucose monitoring throughout.
new_diabetes.duration: Glucose improves over weeks to months; this is lifelong management.
new_diabetes.side_effects: Metformin can cause gut upset early (eases with time/food); insulin and some others can cause low blood sugar.
new_diabetes.followup: Regular reviews: HbA1c every few months, plus eye, foot, kidney and blood-pressure checks.
new_diabetes.recovery: Well-controlled when glucose/HbA1c are in target and you feel well. Very high sugar with vomiting/drowsiness is an emergency (DKA).

hypothyroid.confirm: Confirmed with thyroid blood tests (TSH and T4).
hypothyroid.treatment: Thyroid hormone replacement (levothyroxine), taken on an empty stomach, with the dose adjusted to blood tests.
hypothyroid.duration: Symptoms improve over weeks to a couple of months as levels normalise.
hypothyroid.side_effects: Too much replacement causes palpitations and shakiness; the dose is fine-tuned to avoid over- or under-treatment.
hypothyroid.followup: Recheck thyroid levels about 6–8 weeks after any dose change, then yearly once stable.
hypothyroid.recovery: Well when energy, weight and mood settle and bloods are in range. It's usually lifelong but very manageable.

hyperthyroid.confirm: Confirmed with thyroid blood tests; further tests (antibodies, scan) find the cause.
hyperthyroid.treatment: Anti-thyroid medicine to calm the gland, a beta-blocker for symptoms, and sometimes radioiodine or surgery as definitive treatment.
hyperthyroid.duration: Symptoms ease over weeks; definitive treatment is planned by a specialist.
hyperthyroid.side_effects: Anti-thyroid drugs rarely drop white cells — a sore throat/fever on them needs an urgent blood test; beta-blockers can cause tiredness.
hyperthyroid.followup: Regular thyroid bloods to adjust treatment; specialist (endocrine) review.
hyperthyroid.recovery: Controlled as heart rate, weight and anxiety settle and bloods normalise. Eye symptoms need separate specialist care.

hypoglycemia.confirm: Recognised from symptoms with a low glucose reading that improves after sugar.
hypoglycemia.treatment: Immediate fast-acting sugar (juice, glucose), then a longer-acting snack; glucagon for someone who can't swallow. Then find and fix the cause.
hypoglycemia.duration: Symptoms reverse within minutes of sugar; the underlying cause guides prevention.
hypoglycemia.side_effects: Over-treating can swing sugar high; recurrent lows mean a medicine review (especially insulin/sulfonylureas).
hypoglycemia.followup: Review medicines and patterns if lows recur; carry fast sugar and consider a glucose alert plan.
hypoglycemia.recovery: Resolved once glucose and alertness recover. Someone drowsy or unable to swallow needs emergency help and glucagon.

depression.confirm: A clinical assessment using the story and validated questionnaires; bloods to exclude contributors (e.g. thyroid, anaemia).
depression.treatment: Talking therapy (such as CBT), lifestyle and social support for milder cases; antidepressant medicine added for moderate–severe cases; combined care works best.
depression.duration: Therapy and medicines typically take 4–6 weeks to show clear benefit.
depression.side_effects: Antidepressants can cause early nausea, sleep and sometimes mood changes in the first weeks — early review matters; they're stopped gradually, not abruptly.
depression.followup: Early review (1–2 weeks) to check safety and side effects, then regular follow-up; continue treatment well after recovery to prevent relapse.
depression.recovery: Better as mood, sleep, interest and energy return. Any thoughts of self-harm mean reaching out now — crisis lines and urgent care are there for this.

anxiety_disorder.confirm: A clinical assessment with questionnaires; bloods/caffeine/thyroid considered as contributors.
anxiety_disorder.treatment: Talking therapy (CBT is first-line), lifestyle measures (sleep, caffeine, exercise, breathing skills), and medication (often an SSRI-type) for moderate–severe cases.
anxiety_disorder.duration: Therapy skills build over weeks; medicines take 4–6 weeks, sometimes with a brief early increase in anxiety.
anxiety_disorder.side_effects: SSRIs can cause early jitteriness, nausea and sleep changes that usually settle; they're tapered slowly when stopping.
anxiety_disorder.followup: Early review for side effects and safety, then regular follow-up to adjust the plan.
anxiety_disorder.recovery: Better as worry becomes manageable and avoidance eases. Learned skills keep working long-term; relapses respond to the same tools.

panic_attack.confirm: A clinical diagnosis after excluding physical causes when needed (heart, thyroid).
panic_attack.treatment: Learning the cycle and grounding/breathing techniques, CBT for recurrent attacks, and treating any underlying anxiety disorder.
panic_attack.duration: Individual attacks peak within ~10 minutes and pass; the pattern improves with CBT over weeks.
panic_attack.side_effects: Avoid relying on sedatives — they can worsen the cycle long-term; the skills are the durable treatment.
panic_attack.followup: Review if attacks are frequent or life is restricted by avoidance.
panic_attack.recovery: Controlled as attacks become rarer and less frightening. Understanding that an attack is not dangerous is a big part of recovery.

insomnia.confirm: A clinical assessment of sleep patterns and contributors (caffeine, screens, pain, mood, shift work).
insomnia.treatment: Sleep-hygiene and CBT-for-insomnia (the most effective treatment); medicines only short-term and sparingly for specific situations.
insomnia.duration: CBT-I shows benefit over a few weeks and lasts.
insomnia.side_effects: Sleeping tablets cause daytime grogginess and dependence with regular use — they're not a long-term fix.
insomnia.followup: Review to reinforce the plan and address underlying causes (mood, pain, breathing).
insomnia.recovery: Better as sleep becomes reliable without medication. Treating the cause (stress, pain, apnoea) matters most.

anemia.confirm: Confirmed on a full blood count; further tests (iron, B12/folate, and a search for a cause) follow.
anemia.treatment: Treat the cause and replace what's missing — iron for iron-deficiency, B12/folate injections or tablets as needed; occasionally transfusion if severe.
anemia.duration: Energy improves over weeks; blood counts recover over 1–3 months on treatment.
anemia.side_effects: Iron tablets commonly cause constipation and dark stools; taking with vitamin C and not with tea helps absorption.
anemia.followup: Repeat blood counts to confirm recovery, and investigate the cause (especially iron deficiency in adults — the bowel is checked).
anemia.recovery: Recovered when counts normalise and energy returns. Finding why you became anaemic is as important as the iron itself.

iron_deficiency.confirm: Confirmed with blood count and iron studies (ferritin); the cause (diet, periods, gut loss) is sought.
iron_deficiency.treatment: Iron replacement (tablets usually; infusion if not tolerated or absorbed), plus treating the source of loss and iron-rich foods.
iron_deficiency.duration: Ferritin rebuilds over about 3 months; continue iron a while after levels normalise to restock stores.
iron_deficiency.side_effects: Iron tablets cause constipation, dark stools and nausea — alternate-day dosing can help absorption and tolerance.
iron_deficiency.followup: Recheck iron and blood count; in adults, bowel investigation looks for a hidden source of loss.
iron_deficiency.recovery: Recovered when stores and counts are restored. Treating only the iron without finding the cause risks it returning.

dehydration.confirm: Recognised clinically (thirst, dark urine, dizziness, dry mouth); bloods for severe cases.
dehydration.treatment: Oral rehydration with fluids and salts for mild–moderate cases; IV fluids in hospital for severe dehydration. Treat the cause (vomiting, diarrhoea, heat).
dehydration.duration: Mild dehydration corrects within hours of steady fluids.
dehydration.side_effects: Plain water alone isn't ideal for big losses — rehydration salts replace sodium and glucose too.
dehydration.followup: Re-check for little/no urine, confusion or dizziness on standing (needs urgent care).
dehydration.recovery: Recovered when urine lightens and energy returns. Babies, older and frail people need a low threshold for medical help.

mono.confirm: Suspected from sore throat, big glands and fatigue; a blood test (monospot/EBV) confirms it.
mono.treatment: Supportive care — rest, fluids and pain/fever relief. Antibiotics don't help and a particular one can cause a rash in mono.
mono.duration: The acute illness lasts about 2 weeks; fatigue can linger for weeks to a couple of months.
mono.side_effects: Avoid contact sport for several weeks because the spleen can enlarge and is at risk of injury.
mono.followup: Review for severe swallowing/breathing trouble, tummy pain (spleen), or prolonged symptoms.
mono.recovery: Recovered as energy returns gradually. Don't rush back to heavy exercise until cleared, to protect the spleen.

vitd_deficiency.confirm: Confirmed with a vitamin D blood test; calcium and related levels checked.
vitd_deficiency.treatment: Vitamin D supplementation (a loading course then maintenance), sensible sun exposure and dietary sources.
vitd_deficiency.duration: Levels rebuild over 2–3 months; aches and fatigue ease gradually.
vitd_deficiency.side_effects: Vitamin D is safe at recommended doses; very high self-dosing can raise calcium harmfully, so follow the recommended amount.
vitd_deficiency.followup: Recheck levels after the loading course if symptoms were significant, then maintain.
vitd_deficiency.recovery: Better as levels normalise and symptoms (aches, tiredness) lift. Maintenance keeps it from returning, especially in winter.

conjunctivitis.confirm: A clinical diagnosis distinguishing viral, bacterial and allergic types.
conjunctivitis.treatment: Most viral and mild bacterial cases settle with hygiene and lubricating drops; antibiotic drops for clearly bacterial cases; antihistamine drops for allergic.
conjunctivitis.duration: Viral cases clear over 1–2 weeks; bacterial cases improve within days on drops.
conjunctivitis.side_effects: Antibiotic drops can sting; it's contagious, so handwashing and not sharing towels matter.
conjunctivitis.followup: Review for eye pain, light sensitivity or vision change (not simple conjunctivitis — needs urgent eye assessment).
conjunctivitis.recovery: Resolved when redness and discharge clear. Pain or blurred vision means a different, more serious problem — be seen.

otitis_media.confirm: A clinical diagnosis using an otoscope to view the eardrum.
otitis_media.treatment: Pain relief and fluids first — many clear on their own; antibiotics for younger children, severe cases, or no improvement in 2–3 days.
otitis_media.duration: Pain usually settles within a few days.
otitis_media.side_effects: Antibiotics (if used) can cause diarrhoea; a brief ear discharge can occur if the drum bursts and usually heals.
otitis_media.followup: Review if pain persists beyond a few days, hearing stays down for weeks, or infections keep recurring.
otitis_media.recovery: Better as pain and fever settle. Persistent hearing loss ('glue ear') after infections is checked and followed up.

epistaxis.confirm: A clinical assessment to find the bleeding point and any cause (dryness, medicines, blood pressure).
epistaxis.treatment: First aid — lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose for 10–15 minutes. Persistent bleeds may need cautery or packing; treat dryness afterwards.
epistaxis.duration: Most nosebleeds stop within 10–20 minutes of correct pressure.
epistaxis.side_effects: Cautery can leave the nose tender; moisturising ointment prevents recrudescence; avoid picking and heavy nose-blowing after.
epistaxis.followup: Review for bleeds that won't stop after 20 minutes of pressure, frequent heavy bleeds, or if on blood thinners.
epistaxis.recovery: Resolved when bleeding stops and the lining heals. Heavy bleeding that won't stop, or feeling faint, needs urgent care.

hypertensive_urgency.confirm: Confirmed with repeated blood-pressure readings; checks for organ effects (heart, kidneys, eyes).
hypertensive_urgency.treatment: Gradual, controlled lowering of blood pressure — usually by starting or adjusting regular medicines, not sudden drops; treat any cause. Emergency symptoms mean hospital care.
hypertensive_urgency.duration: Blood pressure is brought down over days to weeks (not minutes) unless there are emergency features.
hypertensive_urgency.side_effects: Blood-pressure medicines can cause dizziness, ankle swelling or a cough depending on the class; the regimen is tailored.
hypertensive_urgency.followup: Close follow-up to confirm control and monitor kidneys and blood tests; home readings help.
hypertensive_urgency.recovery: Controlled as readings reach target without side effects. Chest pain, severe headache, breathlessness or neurological signs are an emergency.

afib.confirm: Confirmed on an ECG; bloods (thyroid, electrolytes) and sometimes a heart scan find contributors.
afib.treatment: Two aims: control the rate/rhythm (medicines or a procedure) and prevent stroke (blood thinner if risk warrants). Treat triggers (thyroid, alcohol, sleep apnoea).
afib.duration: Rate control helps within days; a rhythm/ablation plan is specialist-led over weeks to months.
afib.side_effects: Blood thinners raise bleeding risk and need the right choice/monitoring; rate-control drugs can cause tiredness or a slow pulse.
afib.followup: Regular review of rate, symptoms and stroke-prevention; monitoring for the chosen blood thinner.
afib.recovery: Managed when the rate is controlled, symptoms settle and stroke risk is covered. Sudden breathlessness, chest pain or fainting needs urgent care.

angina_stable.confirm: From exertional chest tightness; confirmed with ECG, blood tests and stress or imaging tests; sometimes angiography.
angina_stable.treatment: Medicines to protect the heart and ease symptoms (a quick-relief nitrate spray, plus heart-rate/blood-flow and risk-lowering drugs), and procedures (stent or bypass) for significant narrowing. Risk-factor control throughout.
angina_stable.duration: Symptom medicines help quickly; the prevention plan is long-term.
angina_stable.side_effects: Nitrates can cause headache and light-headedness; other heart drugs can slow the pulse or lower blood pressure.
angina_stable.followup: Cardiology review, risk-factor targets (blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking, diabetes) and a plan for what to do during an attack.
angina_stable.recovery: Stable when symptoms are predictable and controlled. Chest pain at rest, or pain not easing with rest/spray, is treated as a possible heart attack — call emergency services.

heart_failure.confirm: Confirmed with an echocardiogram, a blood marker (BNP) and clinical signs; the cause is sought.
heart_failure.treatment: Medicines that improve survival and symptoms (several classes used together), fluid/salt management with diuretics, and treating the underlying cause; devices for selected patients.
heart_failure.duration: Symptoms improve over weeks as medicines are built up; this is long-term care.
heart_failure.side_effects: Diuretics can affect kidneys and salts; the core medicines are increased slowly with blood-pressure and blood-test monitoring.
heart_failure.followup: Regular review with weight monitoring (a quick weight gain signals fluid), blood tests and medicine up-titration.
heart_failure.recovery: Managed when breathing, swelling and energy are stable on treatment. Rapid weight gain, worsening breathlessness or swelling needs prompt review.

anaphylaxis.confirm: A clinical emergency diagnosis — sudden breathing, throat, skin and circulation symptoms after a trigger.
anaphylaxis.treatment: Adrenaline (epinephrine) auto-injector into the outer thigh immediately, call emergency services, lie flat with legs raised; repeat adrenaline if needed. Hospital observation follows.
anaphylaxis.duration: Adrenaline works within minutes; observation is needed because symptoms can return hours later.
anaphylaxis.side_effects: Adrenaline can cause a racing heart and shakiness — that's expected and far safer than withholding it.
anaphylaxis.followup: Allergy-clinic referral, an adrenaline auto-injector prescription and a written action plan; carry two devices.
anaphylaxis.recovery: The rule is adrenaline first, questions later — never wait. After recovery, trigger avoidance and carrying auto-injectors prevents the next one.

pulmonary_embolism.confirm: Confirmed in hospital with a blood test (D-dimer) and usually a CT scan of the lung arteries (CTPA) or a lung perfusion scan; an ultrasound may check the leg for a clot.
pulmonary_embolism.treatment: Treated with blood-thinning medicine (anticoagulation); a large, life-threatening clot may need clot-busting drugs or a procedure. This is hospital care, not something to manage at home.
pulmonary_embolism.duration: Blood thinners are usually taken for at least 3 months, sometimes longer or lifelong depending on the cause.
pulmonary_embolism.side_effects: Blood thinners raise the risk of bleeding — report unusual bruising, black or bloody stools, or heavy bleeding. Some types need regular blood tests.
pulmonary_embolism.followup: Follow-up checks the dose and looks for an underlying cause. Seek urgent help if breathlessness or chest pain returns.
pulmonary_embolism.recovery: Many people recover fully over weeks to months; some have lingering breathlessness. Preventing future clots — moving on long trips, staying active after surgery — matters.

cauda_equina.confirm: Confirmed urgently with an MRI scan of the spine; a bladder scan may check how well the bladder empties.
cauda_equina.treatment: Usually emergency surgery to take pressure off the nerves (decompression), ideally within hours. Hospital care.
cauda_equina.duration: Surgery is prompt; recovery of nerve function depends on how quickly the pressure was relieved and can take months.
cauda_equina.side_effects: Surgery carries the usual risks; some bladder, bowel or sexual symptoms can persist despite a good operation.
cauda_equina.followup: Follow-up with spinal, urology and physiotherapy teams, often with bladder and bowel rehabilitation.
cauda_equina.recovery: The earlier the pressure is relieved, the better the chance of recovery; outcomes range from full recovery to lasting changes.

testicular_torsion.confirm: Often diagnosed from the story and examination; an urgent ultrasound may check blood flow, but treatment should not be delayed for tests when torsion is strongly suspected.
testicular_torsion.treatment: Emergency surgery to untwist and stitch the testicle in place (and usually the other side too). Hospital care.
testicular_torsion.duration: Surgery is immediate; recovery from the operation takes about two weeks.
testicular_torsion.side_effects: If the blood supply was cut off for too long the testicle may not survive and may need to be removed; surgery carries the usual risks.
testicular_torsion.followup: A follow-up checks healing; fertility is usually preserved when the other testicle is healthy.
testicular_torsion.recovery: Full recovery is common when treated quickly; fixing both testicles lowers the chance of it happening again.

nec_fasc.confirm: Diagnosed urgently by surgeons; blood tests and scans support it, but an operation to look at the tissue is often both the test and the treatment.
nec_fasc.treatment: Emergency surgery to remove dead tissue, strong antibiotics into a vein, and intensive-care support. Hospital care.
nec_fasc.duration: Often several operations and weeks in hospital; some people need skin grafts.
nec_fasc.side_effects: Major surgery with possible tissue or limb loss and a long recovery.
nec_fasc.followup: Follow-up with surgical, wound-care and rehabilitation teams.
nec_fasc.recovery: Survival and recovery depend heavily on how fast treatment started; rehabilitation can be lengthy.

ectopic.confirm: Confirmed with a pregnancy blood test (hCG, often repeated) and a transvaginal ultrasound; sometimes a short period of monitoring.
ectopic.treatment: Depending on size and stability: close monitoring, medicine (methotrexate) to stop the pregnancy growing, or surgery (often keyhole). A ruptured ectopic is emergency surgery. Hospital care.
ectopic.duration: Medicine needs weeks of blood-test follow-up; surgical recovery takes about two weeks.
ectopic.side_effects: Methotrexate can cause nausea and means avoiding pregnancy for a few months; surgery carries the usual risks.
ectopic.followup: Blood tests confirm the pregnancy hormone falls to zero; future pregnancies should be checked early.
ectopic.recovery: Most people recover well and many go on to have healthy pregnancies, though the risk of another ectopic is a little higher.

acs.confirm: ECG and blood tests (troponin) in hospital, sometimes followed by angiography to look at the heart's arteries.
acs.treatment: Emergency hospital care: aspirin and other medicines, oxygen if needed, and procedures (a stent) or clot-busting drugs to restore blood flow. Call your local emergency number now.
acs.duration: Hospital stay of a few days; recovery over weeks.
acs.side_effects: Blood thinners raise bleeding risk; procedures carry their own risks.
acs.followup: Cardiology follow-up, cardiac rehabilitation, and control of blood pressure, cholesterol and smoking.
acs.recovery: Many return to normal activity; report any return of chest pain or breathlessness at once.

meningitis.confirm: Urgent hospital assessment, usually with blood tests and a lumbar puncture.
meningitis.treatment: Immediate antibiotics into a vein (plus antivirals if needed) and intensive-care support for severe cases. Call your local emergency number now.
meningitis.duration: Hospital stay of days to weeks depending on severity.
meningitis.side_effects: Some antibiotics can cause reactions; severe disease can leave lasting effects.
meningitis.followup: Follow-up checks hearing, and for any after-effects; close contacts may need preventive antibiotics or vaccination.
meningitis.recovery: Most who are treated early recover well; recovery from severe disease can be slow.

sepsis.confirm: Hospital tests — blood cultures, lactate, and a search for the source of infection.
sepsis.treatment: Urgent antibiotics into a vein, fluids, oxygen and organ support in hospital. Call your local emergency number now.
sepsis.duration: Hospital stay of days to weeks; full recovery can take months.
sepsis.side_effects: Strong antibiotics and intensive care carry risks; some have lasting tiredness ('post-sepsis').
sepsis.followup: Follow-up looks for the source and for after-effects; rehabilitation may be needed.
sepsis.recovery: Early treatment greatly improves survival; recovery of energy can be gradual.

dka.confirm: Hospital blood and urine tests for glucose, ketones and acid levels.
dka.treatment: Hospital treatment with fluids into a vein, insulin, and careful replacement of salts. Call your local emergency number now.
dka.duration: Usually a hospital stay of one to several days.
dka.side_effects: Blood sugar and potassium need close monitoring during treatment.
dka.followup: Diabetes-team review of insulin and sick-day rules to prevent it happening again.
dka.recovery: People recover fully with prompt treatment; learning the early warning signs helps prevent a repeat.

heat_stroke.confirm: Recognised from a very high body temperature with confusion or collapse after heat exposure.
heat_stroke.treatment: Rapid cooling and fluids in hospital; organ support if needed. Call your local emergency number now and start cooling meanwhile.
heat_stroke.side_effects: Very high temperatures can injure organs.
heat_stroke.followup: Follow-up checks organ function; avoid further heat until cleared.
heat_stroke.recovery: Prompt cooling is life-saving; recovery depends on how high and how long the temperature ran.

hypothermia.confirm: Recognised from a low body temperature with shivering, confusion or drowsiness after cold exposure.
hypothermia.treatment: Gentle warming and hospital monitoring (the heart is sensitive when cold). Call your local emergency number; warm gently and handle the person carefully.
hypothermia.side_effects: Rapid or rough handling can trigger dangerous heart rhythms.
hypothermia.followup: Follow-up checks for complications and addresses why it happened.

acute_glaucoma.confirm: Urgent eye assessment measuring the pressure inside the eye.
acute_glaucoma.treatment: Emergency eye-clinic treatment: drops and medicines to lower the pressure, then often laser. Seek emergency eye care now — sightsaving is time-critical.
acute_glaucoma.duration: Treatment is urgent; the laser is quick.
acute_glaucoma.side_effects: Pressure-lowering medicines have side effects; discuss with the eye team.
acute_glaucoma.followup: Eye-clinic follow-up, and treatment of the other eye to prevent an attack.
acute_glaucoma.recovery: Vision is usually preserved if treated quickly; delay risks lasting loss.

aortic_dissection.confirm: Hospital imaging (usually a CT scan) of the main artery.
aortic_dissection.treatment: Emergency hospital care — blood-pressure control and often urgent surgery. Call your local emergency number now.
aortic_dissection.side_effects: Surgery and blood-pressure drugs carry significant risks.
aortic_dissection.followup: Lifelong blood-pressure control and scan follow-up.
aortic_dissection.recovery: Survival depends on speed of treatment; recovery from surgery is lengthy.

co_poisoning.confirm: A blood test for carbon-monoxide levels; the story (several people or pets affected, better away from home) is a strong clue.
co_poisoning.treatment: Get into fresh air at once and call your local emergency number; hospital gives high-flow oxygen.
co_poisoning.duration: Oxygen for hours; symptoms may linger.
co_poisoning.side_effects: High levels can affect the heart and brain.
co_poisoning.followup: Have the source (boiler, heater, exhaust) checked and fit a CO alarm before returning.
co_poisoning.recovery: Most recover with oxygen; some have delayed symptoms, so follow-up matters.

opioid_overdose.confirm: Recognised from very slow or stopped breathing, pinpoint pupils and unresponsiveness.
opioid_overdose.treatment: Call your local emergency number now; give naloxone if available and rescue breaths; stay until help arrives.
opioid_overdose.duration: Naloxone works within minutes but can wear off before the opioid does.
opioid_overdose.side_effects: Naloxone can trigger sudden withdrawal; repeat doses may be needed.
opioid_overdose.followup: After recovery, offer links to addiction support and a take-home naloxone kit.
opioid_overdose.recovery: Breathing usually returns with naloxone; the person still needs hospital review as it can wear off.

poisoning_overdose.confirm: Hospital assessment; what and how much was taken, and when, guides treatment.
poisoning_overdose.treatment: Call your local emergency number or Poison Control now; keep packaging. Hospital may give antidotes, charcoal or supportive care. Do not make the person vomit.
poisoning_overdose.side_effects: Varies with the poison and antidote.
poisoning_overdose.followup: Mental-health support if the overdose was intentional.
poisoning_overdose.recovery: Many recover fully with prompt treatment; some poisons act with delay, so early help is vital.

snakebite.confirm: Hospital identifies the bite and watches for venom effects.
snakebite.treatment: Keep still and calm, keep the limb below the heart, remove tight items, and get to hospital fast; antivenom is given if needed. Don't cut, suck or use a tourniquet.
snakebite.duration: Hospital observation for hours; antivenom as needed.
snakebite.side_effects: Antivenom can cause reactions, given under supervision.
snakebite.followup: Wound care and a tetanus check.
snakebite.recovery: Most recover with prompt care; outcome depends on the snake and the time to treatment.

septic_arthritis.confirm: Hospital test drawing fluid from the joint, plus blood tests.
septic_arthritis.treatment: Hospital antibiotics into a vein and often washing out the joint. Seek emergency care now.
septic_arthritis.duration: Hospital stay of days; antibiotics for weeks.
septic_arthritis.side_effects: Prolonged antibiotics and joint washout carry risks.
septic_arthritis.recovery: Early treatment protects the joint; delay can cause lasting damage.

gbs.confirm: Hospital nerve tests and sometimes a lumbar puncture.
gbs.treatment: Hospital treatment (immunoglobulin or plasma exchange) and close monitoring of breathing. Seek emergency care now.
gbs.duration: Weeks in hospital; recovery over months.
gbs.side_effects: Treatments and immobility carry risks; breathing may need support.
gbs.recovery: Most improve substantially, though recovery can be slow.

addisonian_crisis.treatment: Emergency steroids (hydrocortisone) and fluids into a vein. Call your local emergency number now.
addisonian_crisis.followup: Endocrine follow-up, a steroid emergency card and sick-day dosing education.
addisonian_crisis.recovery: People recover quickly with steroids; prevention of future crises is key.

burn_major.confirm: Hospital assessment of burn depth and area.
burn_major.treatment: Emergency care: cool the burn with running water, cover loosely, and call your local emergency number. Hospital gives fluids, pain relief and wound/graft care.
burn_major.duration: Hospital stay and healing over weeks to months.
burn_major.side_effects: Infection and scarring risks; grafts may be needed.
burn_major.recovery: Recovery depends on size and depth; rehabilitation can be lengthy.

retinal_detachment.confirm: Urgent eye examination of the retina.
retinal_detachment.treatment: Urgent eye surgery (laser or an operation) to reattach the retina. Seek emergency eye care now.
retinal_detachment.duration: Surgery is prompt; vision settles over weeks.
retinal_detachment.side_effects: Surgery carries risks; some vision change may remain.
retinal_detachment.recovery: The sooner it is fixed, the better the chance of saving sight.

labor.confirm: Recognised from regular strengthening contractions, waters breaking, or a 'show'.
labor.treatment: Maternity care: contact your midwife or maternity unit. Call emergency services for very fast labour, heavy bleeding, or the baby's cord or a limb showing.
labor.followup: Routine postnatal checks for parent and baby.
labor.recovery: Most labours proceed safely with maternity support.

threatened_miscarriage.confirm: Assessed with a pregnancy review and usually an ultrasound.
threatened_miscarriage.treatment: Seek same-day assessment (early-pregnancy unit). Heavy bleeding with faintness is an emergency — call your local emergency number.
threatened_miscarriage.recovery: Many pregnancies with early bleeding continue; support matters whatever the outcome.

hyperemesis.confirm: Assessed for dehydration and ketones in pregnancy.
hyperemesis.treatment: Hospital or day-unit fluids into a vein and anti-sickness medicine safe in pregnancy.
hyperemesis.duration: May settle over weeks; some need repeated treatment.
hyperemesis.side_effects: Anti-sickness medicines are chosen for pregnancy safety.
hyperemesis.followup: Maternity follow-up and monitoring of weight and hydration.

febrile_seizure.confirm: Recognised from a short seizure during a fever in a young child.
febrile_seizure.treatment: Keep the child safe on their side, time the seizure, and call emergency services if it lasts over 5 minutes or they don't recover. Treat the fever and find its cause.
febrile_seizure.duration: Most last under a few minutes.
febrile_seizure.followup: A doctor should check the cause of the fever.
febrile_seizure.recovery: Simple febrile seizures are usually harmless and most children grow out of them.

bronchiolitis.confirm: Recognised in infants from a cold leading to fast, wheezy, laboured breathing and feeding trouble.
bronchiolitis.treatment: Mostly supportive — small frequent feeds and monitoring. Seek emergency care for fast or struggling breathing, pauses in breathing, or poor feeding/fewer wet nappies.
bronchiolitis.followup: Re-check if breathing worsens or feeding drops.
bronchiolitis.recovery: Most infants recover fully at home; a few need hospital oxygen or feeding support.

alcohol_withdrawal.confirm: Assessed from the drinking history and symptoms (tremor, sweats, agitation).
alcohol_withdrawal.treatment: Medically supervised withdrawal with medicines (benzodiazepines) and vitamins; severe withdrawal (fits, confusion) is an emergency — call your local emergency number.
alcohol_withdrawal.side_effects: Withdrawal medicines are used short-term under supervision.
alcohol_withdrawal.followup: Links to alcohol support and relapse prevention.
alcohol_withdrawal.recovery: Safe withdrawal is very achievable with support; going it alone can be dangerous.

heat_exhaustion.confirm: Recognised from heavy sweating, feeling faint, headache and nausea in the heat.
heat_exhaustion.treatment: Move to a cool place, lie down, raise the legs, sip fluids, and cool the skin. If no better in 30 minutes, or confusion/collapse develops, call your local emergency number (heat stroke).
heat_exhaustion.duration: Usually improves within 30 minutes of cooling.
heat_exhaustion.followup: Rest and rehydrate; avoid further heat that day.
heat_exhaustion.recovery: Full recovery is usual if cooled early.

frostbite.confirm: Recognised from cold, hard, white or numb skin after cold exposure.
frostbite.treatment: Get out of the cold; rewarm gently in warm (not hot) water; do not rub or refreeze. Seek urgent care — deep frostbite needs hospital treatment.
frostbite.duration: Rewarming takes 30+ minutes; healing over weeks.
frostbite.side_effects: Rewarming can be painful; deep injury may lose tissue.
frostbite.followup: Wound care and follow-up for deeper injury.
frostbite.recovery: Superficial frostbite recovers; deep frostbite can cause lasting damage.

travel_fever.confirm: Assessed with blood tests (malaria must be excluded) based on where you travelled.
travel_fever.treatment: See a doctor urgently; some travel infections (like malaria) need specific prompt treatment.
travel_fever.side_effects: Varies with the diagnosis and medicines.
travel_fever.followup: Follow-up with results; tell any clinician your travel history.
travel_fever.recovery: Most travel fevers are treatable, especially when caught early.

animal_bite.confirm: Assessed for wound depth, infection and tetanus/rabies risk.
animal_bite.treatment: Clean the wound well with running water and soap; see a clinician — antibiotics, a tetanus booster, or rabies prevention may be needed.
animal_bite.duration: Wound heals over days to weeks.
animal_bite.followup: Wound re-check; watch for spreading redness.
animal_bite.recovery: Most bites heal well with cleaning and the right prevention.

dvt.confirm: An ultrasound of the leg and a blood test (D-dimer).
dvt.treatment: Blood-thinning medicine (anticoagulation); seek same-day assessment. Sudden breathlessness or chest pain means a possible clot to the lungs — call emergency services.
dvt.duration: Blood thinners for at least 3 months.
dvt.side_effects: Blood thinners raise bleeding risk; report unusual bleeding or bruising.
dvt.followup: Dose checks and a look for an underlying cause.
dvt.recovery: Most clots resolve on treatment; some leave leg swelling or aching.

seizure.confirm: Assessed from the description; tests may include brain imaging and an EEG.
seizure.treatment: Protect the person, cushion the head, don't restrain or put anything in the mouth, time it, and call emergency services if it lasts over 5 minutes, repeats, or is a first seizure.
seizure.side_effects: Anti-seizure medicines (if started) have side effects discussed with a specialist.
seizure.followup: Neurology follow-up; driving and safety advice.
seizure.recovery: Many causes are treatable; a single seizure does not always mean epilepsy.

burn.confirm: Assessed by size, depth and location.
burn.treatment: Cool under running water for 20 minutes, remove jewellery, cover loosely with cling film or a clean non-fluffy cloth; see a clinician for anything larger than a coin, deep, or on the face, hands or genitals.
burn.side_effects: Infection risk; blisters should not be burst.
burn.followup: Dressing changes and a wound re-check.
burn.recovery: Superficial burns heal well; deeper burns may scar and need specialist care.

ptsd.confirm: Recognised from re-experiencing, avoidance and being on edge after trauma.
ptsd.treatment: Trauma-focused talking therapy (such as CBT or EMDR) is first-line; some benefit from medication. A mental-health service can guide this.
ptsd.duration: Therapy runs over weeks to months.
ptsd.side_effects: Any medication's effects are reviewed with the prescriber.
ptsd.followup: Regular therapy review; crisis support if distress peaks.
ptsd.recovery: Many people improve markedly with the right therapy.

grief.confirm: A normal, if painful, response to loss — not an illness.
grief.treatment: Support from people you trust, routines, and time; bereavement counselling helps many. Seek help if grief feels stuck, or with thoughts of self-harm.
grief.duration: Grief eases gradually and in waves, over months.
grief.followup: Check in with yourself and loved ones; counselling if needed.
grief.recovery: There is no fixed timeline; support helps you carry it.

pleurisy.confirm: Recognised from sharp chest pain worse on breathing; a clinician checks for a cause.
pleurisy.treatment: Treat the underlying cause (often a viral infection); anti-inflammatory pain relief helps. Sudden breathlessness needs urgent review (to exclude a clot).
pleurisy.duration: Often settles over 1–2 weeks with the cause.
pleurisy.followup: Re-check if breathless or not improving.
pleurisy.recovery: Most cases settle once the cause is treated.

tb.confirm: Tests include a chest X-ray and sputum samples; see a doctor.
tb.treatment: A supervised course of several antibiotics for months; TB services coordinate care and trace contacts.
tb.duration: Treatment usually lasts at least 6 months.
tb.side_effects: TB antibiotics can affect the liver and eyes; monitored during treatment.
tb.followup: Regular follow-up to confirm cure and support adherence.
tb.recovery: TB is curable with the full course; stopping early risks resistance.

pericarditis.confirm: Assessed with an ECG and sometimes an ultrasound of the heart.
pericarditis.treatment: Anti-inflammatory medicines (and colchicine); see a clinician. Severe breathlessness or faintness needs emergency care.
